notes.1a: Nearly all candidates identified the stirring rod and Bunsen burner correctly.
notes.1b: Whilst most candidates could answer this question correctly, there was some confusion between the terms solvent, solute and solution. Other candidates gave specific examples.
notes.1c: Many candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.1d: Most candidates realised that the water had evaporated, although a few thought that it had been filtered out.
notes.2a: The most common incorrect response, often concentrated on the comparative lengths of the various tubes and the use of a tap funnel, sometimes mistaken for a burette, for the delivery of the hydrochloric acid.
notes.2b: Some candidates knew that a fume cupboard (or a well-ventilated area) should be used, although many gave it different names. Other responses concentrated on general safely precautions, such as tying hair back or wearing goggles. The use of gas masks was not credited.
notes.3a: The table of results was usually completed correctly.
notes.3b: Most points were plotted correctly, although many curves were not smooth. There were several straight lines and curves that also went through the anomalous point.
notes.3c: Most responses not only identified the anomalous point, but also explained how they knew that it was anomalous.
notes.3d: The extrapolation of the curve was well attempted by nearly all candidates and most gave a correct reading for the temperature.
notes.3e: The majority of candidates gave a chemical test for water. A large minority, however, gave a physical property as a test for pure water.
notes.4a: Taking readings from the burettes was well attempted by nearly all candidates. However, some responses give the initial volume as “0” rather than “0.0”. A few candidates did not realise that the burette scale reads downwards.
notes.4c: Most candidates realised that iron( II ) was present in Solution E and that it was then oxidised to iron( III ). A few candidates incorrectly thought both were present in the original solution.
notes.4di: Some candidates gave only the final answer, rather than the colour change. The most common error was giving the colour change of the potassium manganate( VII ) at the end-point (purple to pink) rather than the colour change in the conical flask (colourless to pink).
notes.4dii: There were many good reasons stated for not using an indicator.
notes.4e: Most candidates knew that Experiment 2 used the greatest volume and that it was twice as much as Experiment 1. Some responses did not explain why this occurred and confused the strength of the acid with that of the solution. Others found it difficult to say which solution was the most concentrated. The more able candidates realised that Solution E was twice as concentrated as Solution D.
notes.4f: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. A few candidates realised that the volume halved, but did not give an actual volume.
notes.4g: The advantages and disadvantages of using measuring cylinders were well known.
notes.5c: Most candidates realised that there would be no reaction with barium nitrate solution.
notes.5d: The formation of a white precipitate when a chloride reacts with silver nitrate solution was given by most candidates.
notes.5e: Whilst most candidates realised that the solution was neutral, few went on to say that it was a transition element. Other acceptable answers were iron ( III ), a dichromate, a chromate, or methyl orange.
notes.5f: Both reversible and neutralisation were accepted, but the explanation also needed to refer to the information given in the question, in this case the colour changes.
notes.5g: Nearly all candidates correctly identified oxygen.
